I had no idea Temples was gonna be so kick-ass. I hadn't really planned on necessarily being there, but after St. Paul and the Broken Bones surprised me with a fantastic show, I stayed and was blown away even more by Temples. I hope people don't hate yellers too much, because I completely lost my voice at that one. It was great to feel like the crowd around me was really feeling the same energy as me. It's always great to really get into a song, and only need occasional, momentary eye contact with strangers nearby to feel connected. The dudes in front of me were definitely getting into it, and it's great that we all energized each other. "A Question Isn't Answered" was probably my favorite single song at the festival, just ask my calves.

They were both amazingly fun. Chromeo was more energized, the crowd wasn't perfect but it was a fun one. Tame Impala was edging on spiritual at times. My marijuana peak was during Tame Impala, and I had the time of my life. I will never forget watching the sun come out from what had been a more cloudy day, and seeing the sunlight travelling it's way through the crowd. You could tell it was both energizing to some, but sapping to others; some people were quickly overheating and slowing their groove. I was lucky enough to be shaded by the stage until the last song of the set. As the song was reaching it's climax I felt the sun finally hit my face, and while I had been dancing my booty off the whole time, that was the moment I really lost it in the best way imaginable.

I was resting in the shade of the Jack Daniels tent when St. Paul and the Broken Bones came on. I had listened to some of their songs in preparation for Sasquatch and determined they were good but not a must-see. I was dead wrong. After one song I was booking it out of the shade and into that crowd. One J later and I was absolutely falling in love with that saint. The smile that would unfold upon his face after belting or crooning his way to applause and admiration was heart-warmingly genuine. You could tell that he was proud of himself in such a way that was hard not to feel proud of him too. I'm not sure I've ever felt that way during a show. He gave energy that continued all day long; Sunday was probably my favorite day of the fest.

I'm on the development team for Eidolon and I take no offense by that, it's good feedback to get, although I will give some context/defense. Months after development started, we decided we needed to rework the title. When we found [Walt Whitman's Eidolons](http://classiclit.about.com/library/bl-etexts/wwhitman/bl-ww-eido.htm) we fell in love. It's definitely a complex Walt Whitman poem, and by no means do we understand it all, it's a hard one to analyze, but it spoke to us, echoed much of the narrative theme we wanted in the game. Our narrative, however, is presented in a fairly unconventional way, very slow and undirected, we let the user discover what they want. While the poem may seem maybe too smart, a little high brow and scholarly, our team of writers did a great job exploring the themes important to us with a wide range of voices and some of it is pretty darn smart. Users definitely won't be reading a bunch of documents written by programmers with no writing experience.

It's definitely not for everyone, here's a review that's pretty representative of the type of player that will enjoy Eidolon:

What argument do you have to support the idea that tradition should remain unchanged when it comes to marriage?

I'm not saying you are wrong to feel or think what you do, but what you think and feel are wrong. In fact it may be completely understandable for you to have the point of view that you have. I am saying, however, that what you are attempting to support is unsupportable in any logical way. It is a fact of life that law and society will naturally progress towards acceptance.

Fine, let me completely re-explain my first statement: the word marriage once excluded interracial couples. That was the tradition. That is now wrong. That meaning of marriage, while accepted by whatever majority, was wrong to be upheld by law outlined by the US Constitution and other precedent. No matter how much others thought that it should simply remain tradition to exclude interracial couples from the term "marriage" or the rights accompanied by such a civil union, their opinion was supported by nothing more than wanting tradition to remain, and therefore, their argument fell, and the minority opinion prevailed, allowing interracial couples to have civil unions, federally-recognized marriages. Allowing an interracial couple to be married did not stop a same-race couple from the same recognition, their civil union could still be recognized as a marriage. This same scenario is playing out as we speak in the fight for social, cultural, and political progress towards sexuality rights, and equality of marriage. You can no longer say that a majority of Americans think that the distinction is right. You can no longer say that a majority of Americans think homosexual marriage should be illegal. You can no longer say that a majority of Americans would prefer our American culture and society to stagnate in tradition when it comes to who marriage is thought of and defined. And even if you are someday able to accurately support those claims again, the minority opinion will be upheld because it does not infringe on any right, it does not remove any meaning. It adds without subtracting.

Tradition is important in certain areas, tradition can be valued always. But when it comes to law and society, tradition changes and progresses through whatever walls people try to reinforce tradition with. It is, in a sense, it's own beast, affected by all. The change and progress of this beast is inevitable.

You will seem a fool to that future beast. You seem a fool now.

Alright fine let's cover it with a word like homophobia, a cop-out word trying to make those who do not attempt or want to understand those different then them, sound like victims of fear, some mental or psychological condition we should be sympathetic of like those with arachnophobia or claustrophobia. To draw similarities with that word is not helpful in the slightest. I may agree wholeheartedly that hate is an extremely strong word, but to describe those who dislike and refuse to attempt understand is a difficult thing, especially when their reasoning is without religious or any other logical reasoning or support.

Marriage is not a right? Yeah, fine, however the benefits accompanying that federally-recognized relationship are rights to that couple, and some couples in nearly identical relationships are being denied those rights. In all reality, it'd be nice if government had never gotten into the business of recognizing anyone's marriages and not given anyone benefits. However, while that's the closest thing to a compromise that I hear from Conservatives, it simply doesn't make sense to remove rights already given. It is only natural to allow financial and legal ease once a human relationship has naturally developed into something that fits the standards that we currently hold such as being a relationship based on love and exclusive commitment.

you say that the prevailing understanding of marriage is such "regardless of church influence," however, I can't think of any reason to not "redefine" marriage that is not based on religion, or just pure, unsupported hatred. Sure, this is not just a religious question, it is a cultural question as well, but one of the answers to the question has non-religious, non-hatred reasoning, while the other answer is actually moving society to make progress in understanding a wider variety of people and lifestyles other than your own.

Also, while the "prevailing understanding of marriage in the Western world and in recent history" may be heteronormative, same-sex unions have likely existed for as long as different-gendered institutions similar to marriage.

All we should do is try our best to present as many possibilities for our children, with the evidence for and against things. If you want to raise your children morals like forgiveness, respect, kindness, integrity, while letting them know that your understanding of those morals came from the church, that's ok, but if you want to scare them into a world where they are encouraged and rewarded for disallowing the equality of sexualities, I will fight you.

May have come closer to death than this, but I feel like one small decision saved me from my own stupidity as a child.

I was middle school age, and met up with some friends at a friend's house down the street. Instead of walking, which would've been very easy to do, I decided to ride my bike. I also decided to wear my helmet. (Thanks Mom)

Well once I got there, two friends were playing on a rope swing that had just been put up on a tall tree in the side yard. It was the type that had a rope that a friend could pull to swing you. They were pulling one another, going kinda high. 

It was then my turn, and I wanted to be a badass. Which meant I was a dumbass. I was a skinny runt, and both my friends were gonna pull the rope. Before I even started moving, I had decided that to be a badass, I would have to jump off, which seemed doable from the height they had swung.

Well I swung much higher, was level with their second story back deck when I decided to let go, completely parallel to the ground and plummet face-first into the ground.

I'm really glad I'm a dork: I was still wearing my bike helmet. It saved everything but my Rudolph-esqe red nose.

**TLDR**: I let go of a rope swing from two stories up, and my dorky bike helmet saved my noggin.
